chunks: Where to sense buck output current. The question: When should output current be sensed? Before or after the output inductor? Or somewhere else?
You can measure a buck's current at different places, and the place depends on the purpose.
Near the inductor or switch, you get the fast, rippling current that control and protection need.
At the output, in series with the load, you get the smooth, slower current that metering and accuracy need.
Think of a river feeding a reservoir, with a steady stream leaving it. Upstream of the reservoir the flow surges and dips with each pulse of the pump.
Downstream, the reservoir has smoothed it into a steady flow. If you want to react to each surge, measure upstream. If you want the real consumption, measure downstream.
The picture leaves out one cost: a sensor in the outflow sits in the load's path and drops a little voltage itself.
Five places to put a sensing element. A (high-side FET) and D (low-side FET) see pulsed halves of the inductor current.
B (inductor, by DCR or a series shunt) sees the whole triangle. C (a shunt after the output capacitor) sees smooth DC. E (the input) sees chopped current filtered by C in .
Each is right for a different job.
Inductor current: the actual current in the power stage; it ramps up and down ("Why inductor current is a linear ramp"). Ripple: the up-and-down swing of that current each cycle.
Peak current-mode control: a control scheme that turns the switch off when the inductor current reaches a limit ("Voltage mode vs current mode control").
Cycle-by-cycle limit: a protection that checks the current every switching cycle. Common-mode voltage: the average voltage level the sense signal sits on.
A buck feeds a steady 3 amps load, and the inductor ripple is 1 amps peak-to-peak. At the inductor, the current ramps between 2. 5 amps and 3.
5 amps each cycle, so a protection circuit sees the 3. 5 amps peak immediately. In series with the load, after the capacitor, the current is a smooth 3 amps with almost no wobble.
That is the whole idea.
"For control and fast protection I sense the inductor or switch current, before the output capacitor, because that's the real state of the power stage and it isn't filtered yet.
For accurate load current or telemetry I sense after the capacitor in series with the load, where it's smooth DC and the common-mode is just V out .
Sensing right after the inductor still shows the ripple. And the input side is for input current limit. So the location follows the purpose."
